summary: Adds two SIP header fields, Answer-Mode and Priv-Answer-Mode, that an INVITE can use to say whether the called device should wait for the user before answering or answer automatically. The privileged version asks for administrative-level access and so needs extra authentication and authorization. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: When you call someone, you can add a note saying either please wait until a person picks up, or pick up by yourself. A special version of the note is only obeyed if you prove you are allowed to ask.

questions: how to request auto answer in sip
what is the sip answer-mode header
what does the require parameter mean in answer-mode
subtitle: Two SIP header fields that let a caller ask whether the called device should wait for its user or answer on its own.

tldr.problem: SIP had no standard way for a caller to say whether a called device should wait for its user to accept the call or accept automatically, which matters for push-to-talk, loopback tests and intercom-style calls.
tldr.mechanism: An INVITE carries Answer-Mode or Priv-Answer-Mode with the value Manual or Auto, optionally with a require parameter. The called device applies its own authorization policy, and may report how it answered in the 200 (OK) response.
tldr.outcome: The headers are only a request: the called device decides, must not auto-answer where the user's privacy or security would suffer, and the RFC sets a minimal security policy for doing so.

today: RFC 5373 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Ask How a Call Is Answered
sections.content:
In the usual SIP model, an INVITE arrives, the user is notified, the user accepts, and a 200 (OK) response goes back. A called device could always skip the notification and acceptance steps, but a caller had no standard way to ask for that treatment.

The RFC names three scenarios. A testing service may send a diagnostic loopback call that echoes media back for analysis. Push-to-talk calls are conventionally accepted automatically and played on a loudspeaker. A PBX attendant may want intercom behavior for some calls and an ordinary call for others.

The RFC separates answering mode (how the user accepts or rejects a request) from alerting mode (how the user is told, such as a ring tone). Only answering mode is in scope. Answering machines do not need this extension, because they already know they are expected to answer.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a caller wants the phone to pick up by itself, like a walkie-talkie, and sometimes wants a person to decide. This note lets the caller say which one they would like.

sections.title: The Two Header Fields and the Option Tag
sections.content:
The RFC defines Answer-Mode and Priv-Answer-Mode. Both take the value Manual or Auto (or an extension token) and an optional require parameter. The option tag that signals support is answermode.

Names and values are compared case-insensitively. Implementations MUST ignore unknown values, which keeps the syntax open to future extension.

Use is defined only in initial, dialog-forming INVITE requests and in 200 (OK) responses to them. ACK, CANCEL and mid-dialog use such as a re-INVITE are not defined, and the headers in other requests are ignored.
sections.eli5: There are two notes, a normal one and a special one. Each can say wait for a person or pick up automatically. Anyone who does not understand a new kind of note should just ignore it.

sections.title: How Requests Are Made and Handled
sections.content:
Manual asks the called user agent to wait until its user has interacted with the interface to accept. Auto asks it to accept without waiting for the user. If neither header is present, answering is up to the called device, as before.

The require parameter changes what happens when the device will not follow the request. It does not influence the device's choice of mode. It is checked only after the mode is chosen, and if the chosen mode differs from the requested one, the caller is asking the device to reject the call instead of answering in another mode. For example, Auto;require means answer automatically or reject, never answer manually.

A calling client can also add Require: answermode to make the far end either understand the extension or reject, and can use Accept-Contact with an extensions parameter value of answermode so that retargeting proxies prefer or only pick contacts that registered support. A device can advertise support in its REGISTER Contact header, and SHOULD list answermode in the Supported header of its requests.

The called device SHOULD defer a Manual request until the user confirms, and with require it MUST defer or reject. For Auto it SHOULD accept when the caller is authenticated and authorized, and otherwise may treat the call as manual or reject. A rejection SHOULD use 403 (Forbidden), and the RFC suggests reason phrases such as automatic answer forbidden and manual answer forbidden.
sections.eli5: The caller can say wait for a person or pick up yourself. Adding the word require means if you will not do it my way, just do not answer at all instead of doing it your way.

sections.title: Answer-Mode Versus Priv-Answer-Mode
sections.content:
Both headers ask for the same two behaviors. The difference is the policy the called device applies. Priv-Answer-Mode is not a claim of privilege. It is a request for privileged treatment, like running a command with sudo in UNIX, where a separate policy table decides who may.

A device SHOULD apply a stricter policy to Priv-Answer-Mode, and the default SHOULD be to refuse it unless the requester is authenticated and specifically authorized. The RFC uses a limousine driver as an example. His communicator answers push-to-talk calls only manually, so a dispatcher's normal Answer-Mode: Auto calls go unanswered while he sleeps. An urgent call with Priv-Answer-Mode: Auto from an authorized dispatcher is answered at once.

If both headers are present, the device first checks authorization for Priv-Answer-Mode. If the caller qualifies, only that header is processed. Otherwise only Answer-Mode is. Identity checks can use SIP Digest Authentication (RFC 3261), the SIP Identity mechanism (RFC 4474), or asserted identity in trusted networks (RFC 3325).
sections.eli5: The special note is like saying I would like to use my boss pass. The phone checks a list to see if you really are allowed, and the list for special passes is much shorter.

sections.title: Proxies, Forking and Responses
sections.content:
Proxies in general ignore the headers. Serving proxies MAY insert, delete or alter them, but MUST NOT unless the proxy operator and the user it serves have explicitly agreed to it, because the result could surprise users, such as a diagnostic loopback call answered by a human.

Auto-answer makes the multiple acceptance problem worse when a request is forked to several devices, so auto-answer is NOT RECOMMENDED where parallel forking is used. The RFC suggests manual answer with no alerting and early media, or dynamic conferencing, as alternatives.

A device may put the same header with the value Manual or Auto in its 200 (OK) response to show how the call was answered, and the caller MAY use that to adapt its interface. Because this can reveal that a person is present, devices SHOULD have a configurable policy for it, and the default SHOULD be to leave the header out.
sections.eli5: If a call rings many phones and they all pick up by themselves, there is a mess. Also, saying I picked up myself tells the caller a person is nearby, so phones keep that secret unless told otherwise.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Auto-answer is risky. The RFC lists attacks such as turning a phone into a remote listening device, reverse charge fraud, spam over push-to-talk, playing obnoxious noises (the "whoopee cushion" attack), battery run-down, "forced busy" denial of service, and phishing through session insertion.

Since SIP seldom has end-to-end protection, the extension depends on trust across proxies, and any misbehaving proxy can change these headers unnoticed. The RFC sorts media attacks into insertion (media played to the victim) and interception (the victim's microphone or camera activated), and treats the "bug-my-phone" interception case as the more severe one.

The RFC lists five defenses: identity, alerting, acceptance, limiting input and output, and policy. Devices MUST have and use a request-identity mechanism. Its minimal policy says a device SHOULD NOT establish a session with inbound media without explicit user acceptance when the requester is unknown or not authorized. A device MUST NOT establish a session with outbound or bidirectional media sourced from the device without explicit user acceptance, though loopback media for connectivity testing is exempt. If a session began with automatic answering, the device MUST NOT move to sending outbound media without the user's acceptance.
sections.eli5: If any caller could make your phone answer itself, they might listen in or blast noise at you. So the phone must know who is calling, and it must never switch its microphone on by itself.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC adds Answer-Mode and Priv-Answer-Mode to the SIP header field registry, with no compact form. It registers the require parameter for both headers, with no predefined values, and registers the option tag answermode, described as support for negotiating automatic or manual answering of a request.
sections.eli5: The new notes and the support tag were written into the official list of SIP words so nobody else uses the same names.
